### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Practice Set 2.1 Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Question 1.

 Identify, with reason, which of the following are Pythagorean triplets.

 i. (3,5,4)

 ii. (4,9,12)

 iii. (5,12,13)

 iv. (24,70,74)

 v. (10,24,27)

 vi. (11,60,61)

 Solution:

 i. Here, 5 2 = 25

 3 2 + 4 2 = 9 + 16 = 25

 ∴ 5 2 = 3 2 + 4 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ (3,5,4) is a Pythagorean triplet.

ii. Here, 12 2 = 144

 4 2 + 9 2= 16 + 81 =97

 ∴ 12 2 ≠ 4 2 + 92

 The square of the largest number is not equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ (4,9,12) is not a Pythagorean triplet.

iii. Here, 13 2 = 169

 5 2 + 12 2 = 25 + 144 = 169

 ∴ 13 2 = 5 2 + 12 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ (5,12,13) is a Pythagorean triplet.

iv. Here, 74 2 = 5476

 24 2 + 70 2 = 576 + 4900 = 5476

 ∴ 74 2 = 24 2 + 70 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ (24, 70,74) is a Pythagorean triplet.

v. Here, 27 2 = 729

 10 2 + 24 2 = 100 + 576 = 676

 ∴ 27 2 ≠ 10 2 + 24 2

 The square of the largest number is not equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ (10,24,27) is not a Pythagorean triplet.

vi. Here, 61 2 = 3721

 11 2 + 60 2 = 121 + 3600 = 3721

 ∴ 61 2 = 11 2 + 60 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ (11,60,61) is a Pythagorean triplet.

Question 2.

 In the adjoining figure, ∠MNP = 90°, seg NQ ⊥ seg MP,MQ = 9, QP = 4, find NQ.

 Solution:

 ∴ NQ = M Q×Q P−−−−−−−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

Question 3.

 In the adjoining figure, ∠QPR = 90°, seg PM ⊥ seg QR and Q – M – R, PM = 10, QM = 8, find QR.

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-2.png?resize=203%2C134&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 In ∆PQR, ∠QPR = 90° and [Given]

 seg PM ⊥ seg QR

 ∴ PM 2 = OM × MR [Theorem of geometric mean]

 ∴ 10 2 = 8 × MR

 ∴ MR = 100 8

 = 12.5

 Now, QR = QM + MR [Q – M – R]

 = 8 + 12.5

 ∴ QR = 20.5 units

Question 4.

 See adjoining figure. Find RP and PS using the information given in ∆PSR.

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-3.png?resize=208%2C129&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 In ∆PSR, ∠S = 90°, ∠P = 30° [Given]

 ∴ ∠R = 60° [Remaining angle of a triangle]

 ∴ ∆PSR is a 30° – 60° – 90° triangle.

 RS = 1 2 RP [Side opposite to 30°]

 ∴6 = 1 2 RP

 ∴ RP = 6 × 2 = 12 units

 Also, PS = 3√2 RP [Side opposite to 60°]

 = 3√2 × 12

 = 6 3–√ units

 ∴ RP = 12 units, PS = 6 3–√ units

Question 6.

 Find the side and perimeter of a square whose diagonal is 10 cm.

![Image 8: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-11.jpg?resize=143%2C127&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Let ꠸ABCD be the given square.

 l(diagonal AC) = 10 cm

 Let the side of the square be ‘x’ cm.

 In ∆ABC,

 ∠B = 90° [Angle of a square]

 ∴ AC 2 = AB 2 + BC 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 10 2 = x 2 + x 2

 ∴ 100 = 2x 2

 ∴ x 2 = 100 2

 ∴x 2 = 50

 ∴ x = 50−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = =25×2−−−−−√=5 2–√

 ∴side of square is 5 2–√ cm.

Question 7.

 In the adjoining figure, ∠DFE = 90°, FG ⊥ ED. If GD = 8, FG = 12, find

 i. EG

 ii. FD, and

 iii. EF

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-6.png?resize=207%2C107&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 ∴ 122 = 8 × EG .

 ∴ EG = 144 8

 ∴ EG = 18 units

ii. In ∆FGD, ∠FGD = 90° [Given]

 ∴ FD 2 = FG 2 + GD 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 = 122 + 82 = 144 + 64

 = 208

 ∴ FD = 208−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 ∴ FD = 4 13−−√ units

iii. In ∆EGF, ∠EGF = 90° [Given]

 ∴ EF 2 = EG 2 + FG 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 = 182 + 122 = 324 + 144

 ∴ EF = 468−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

Question 8.

 Find the diagonal of a rectangle whose length is 35 cm and breadth is 12 cm.

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-7.png?resize=227%2C105&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Let ꠸ABCD be the given rectangle.

 AB = 12 cm, BC 35 cm

 In ∆ABC, ∠B = 90° [Angle of a rectangle]

 ∴ AC 2 = AB 2 + BC 2[Pythagoras theorem]

 = 122 + 352

 = 144 + 1225

 = 1369

 ∴ AC = 1369−−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = 37 cm

 ∴ The diagonal of the rectangle is 37 cm.

Question 9.

 In the adjoining figure, M is the midpoint of QR. ∠PRQ = 90°.

 Prove that, PQ 2 = 4 PM 2 – 3 PR 2.

![Image 11: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-8.png?resize=217%2C135&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Proof:

 In ∆PQR, ∠PRQ = 90° [Given]

 PQ 2 = PR 2 + QR 2 (i) [Pythagoras theorem]

 RM = 1 2 QR [M is the midpoint of QR]

 ∴ 2RM = QR (ii)

 ∴ PQ 2 = PR 2 + (2RM)2 [From (i) and (ii)]

 ∴ PQ 2 = PR 2 + 4RM 2 (iii)

 Now, in ∆PRM, ∠PRM = 90° [Given]

 ∴ PM 2 = PR 2 + RM 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ RM 2 = PM 2 – PR 2 (iv)

 ∴ PQ 2 = PR 2 + 4 (PM 2 – PR 2) [From (iii) and (iv)]

 ∴ PQ 2 = PR 2 + 4 PM 2 – 4 PR 2

 ∴ PQ 2 = 4 PM 2 – 3 PR 2

Question 10.

 Walls of two buildings on either side of a street are parallel to each other. A ladder 5.8 m long is placed on the street such that its top just reaches the window of a building at the height of 4 m. On turning the ladder over to the other side of the street, its top touches the window of the other building at a height 4.2 m. Find the width of the street.

 Solution:

 Let AC and CE represent the ladder of length 5.8 m, and A and E represent windows of the buildings on the opposite sides of the street. BD is the width of the street.

![Image 12: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-9.png?resize=325%2C135&ssl=1)

 AB = 4 m and ED = 4.2 m

 In ∆ABC, ∠B = 90° [Given]

 AC 2 = AB 2 + BC 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 5.8 2 = 4 2 + BC 2

 ∴ 5.8 2 – 4 2 = BC 2

 ∴ (5.8 – 4) (5.8 + 4) = BC 2

 ∴ 1.8 × 9.8 = BC 2

![Image 13: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Practice Set 2.1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Practice-Set-2.1-10.jpg?resize=598%2C235&ssl=1)

 CE 2 = CD 2 + DE 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 5.8 2 = CD 2 + 4.22

 ∴ 5.8 2 – 4.2 2 = CD 2

 ∴ (5.8 – 4.2) (5.8 + 4.2) = CD 2

 ∴ 1.6 × 10 = CD 2

 ∴ CD 2 = 16

 ∴ CD = 4m (ii) [Taking square root of both sides]

 Now, BD = BC + CD [B – C – D]

 = 4.2 + 4 [From (i) and (ii)]

 = 8.2 m

 ∴ The width of the street is 8.2 metres.

Question 1.

 Verify that (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (24,25,7) are Pythagorean triplets. (Textbook pg. no. 30)

 Solution:

 i. Here, 5 2 = 25

 3 2 + 4 2 = 9 + 16 = 25

 ∴ 5 2 = 3 2 + 4 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ 3,4,5 is a Pythagorean triplet.

ii. Here, 13 2 = 169

 5 2 + 12 2 = 25 + 144 = 169

 ∴ 13 2 = 5 2 + 12 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ 5,12,13 is a Pythagorean triplet.

iii. Here, 17 2 = 289

 8 2 + 15 2 = 64 + 225 = 289

 ∴ 17 2 = 8 2 + 15 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ 8,15,17 is a Pythagorean triplet.

iv. Here, 25 2 = 625

 7 2 + 24 2 = 49 + 576 = 625

 ∴ 25 2 = 7 2 + 24 2

 The square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two numbers.

 ∴ 24,25, 7 is a Pythagorean triplet.

Question 2.

 Assign different values to a and b and obtain 5 Pythagorean triplets. (Textbook pg. no. 31)

 Solution:

 i. Let a = 2, b = 1

 a 2 + b 2 = 2 2 + 1 2 = 4 + 1 = 5

 a 2 – b 2 = 2 2 – 1 2 = 4 – 1 = 3

 2ab = 2 × 2 × 1 = 4

 ∴ (5, 3, 4) is a Pythagorean triplet.

ii. Let a = 4,b = 3

 a 2 + b 2 = 4 2 + 3 2 = 16 + 9 = 25

 a 2 – b 2 = 4 2 – 3 2 = 16 – 9 = 7

 2ab = 2 × 4 × 3 = 24

 ∴ (25, 7, 24) is a Pythagorean triplet.

iii. Let a = 5, b = 2

 a 2 + b 2 = 5 2 + 2 2 = 25 + 4 = 29

 a 2 – b 2 = 5 2 – 2 2 = 25 – 4 = 21

 2ab = 2 × 5 × 2 = 20

 ∴ (29, 21, 20) is a Pythagorean triplet.

iv. Let a = 4,b = 1

 a 2 + b 2 = 4 2 + 1 2 = 16 + 1 = 17

 a 2 – b 2 = 42 – 12 = 16 – 1 = 15

 2ab = 2 × 4 × 1 = 8

 ∴ (17, 15, 8) is a Pythagorean triplet.

v. Let a = 9, b = 7

 a 2 + b 2 = 92 + 72 = 81 + 49 = 130

 a 2 – b 2 = 92 – 72 = 81 – 49 = 32

 2ab = 2 × 9 × 7 = 126

 ∴ (130,32,126) is a Pythagorean triplet.

Note: Numbers in Pythagorean triplet can be written in any order.

Question 1

Identify, with reason, which of the following are Pythagorean triplets.  
i. (3,5,4)  
ii. (4,9,12)  
iii. (5,12,13)  
iv. (24,70,74)  
v. (10,24,27)  
vi. (11,60,61)

Method

For each triple, pick the largest number as the candidate hypotenuse c and the other two as legs a and b. Compute a^2 + b^2 and compare it with c^2. If a^2 + b^2 = c^2, the triple is a Pythagorean triplet.

Working

i. (3, 5, 4)  
- Largest = 5.  
- 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.  
- 5^2 = 25.  
- Since 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2, (3,5,4) is a Pythagorean triplet.

ii. (4, 9, 12)  
- Largest = 12.  
- 4^2 + 9^2 = 16 + 81 = 97.  
- 12^2 = 144.  
- 97 ≠ 144, so (4,9,12) is not a Pythagorean triplet.

iii. (5, 12, 13)  
- Largest = 13.  
- 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169.  
- 13^2 = 169.  
- 5^2 + 12^2 = 13^2, so (5,12,13) is a Pythagorean triplet.

iv. (24, 70, 74)  
- Largest = 74.  
- 24^2 + 70^2 = 576 + 4900 = 5476.  
- 74^2 = 5476.  
- 24^2 + 70^2 = 74^2, so (24,70,74) is a Pythagorean triplet.

v. (10, 24, 27)  
- Largest = 27.  
- 10^2 + 24^2 = 100 + 576 = 676.  
- 27^2 = 729.  
- 676 ≠ 729, so (10,24,27) is not a Pythagorean triplet.

vi. (11, 60, 61)  
- Largest = 61.  
- 11^2 + 60^2 = 121 + 3600 = 3721.  
- 61^2 = 3721.  
- 11^2 + 60^2 = 61^2, so (11,60,61) is a Pythagorean triplet.

Final answer

Pythagorean triplets: (3,5,4), (5,12,13), (24,70,74), (11,60,61).  
Not Pythagorean triplets: (4,9,12), (10,24,27).

Question 2

In the adjoining figure, ∠MNP = 90°, segment NQ ⟂ segment MP, MQ = 9, QP = 4. Find NQ.

Method

Use the property of the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse: in a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse makes two smaller right triangles that are similar to the original triangle and to each other. From that similarity we get the geometric-mean relation
NQ^2 = MQ × QP.
We will apply this relation and compute NQ.

Working

Given MQ = 9 and QP = 4. By the geometric-mean relation for the altitude,
NQ^2 = MQ × QP = 9 × 4 = 36.
Taking square root (positive length),
NQ = √36 = 6.

Final answer

NQ = 6 units.

Question  
In the adjoining figure, ∠QPR = 90°, PM ⟂ QR and Q – M – R, PM = 10, QM = 8. Find QR.

Method  
Use the property of the altitude drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse: in right triangle PQR, with altitude PM to hypotenuse QR (meeting QR at M), we have
PM^2 = QM × MR.
From this relation find MR, then add QM and MR to obtain QR.

Working
1. Apply the altitude property:
   PM^2 = QM × MR

2. Substitute the given values (PM = 10, QM = 8):
   10^2 = 8 × MR
   100 = 8 × MR

3. Solve for MR:
   MR = 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5

4. Find QR as the sum of the two segments on the hypotenuse:
   QR = QM + MR = 8 + 12.5 = 20.5

Final answer  
QR = 20.5 units.

Question
For finding AB and BC with the help of information given in the adjoining figure, complete the following activity.

(Diagram cue: the diagram shows triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AB = BC. No numerical lengths are given on the diagram.)

Method
1. Use the isosceles triangle property: if two sides are equal, the angles opposite them are equal.
2. Use the triangle angle-sum property to find the measures of the angles.
3. Use the Pythagorean theorem to express the equal legs AB and BC in terms of the hypotenuse AC (since no numerical lengths are provided).

Working
1. Given AB = BC, so triangle ABC is isosceles with the equal sides meeting at B. Therefore the base angles are equal:
   ∠BAC = ∠BCA. Let each equal angle be x.

2. Diagram cue gives ∠B = 90°. Using the triangle angle-sum:
   ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°
   x + 90° + x = 180°
   2x + 90° = 180°
   2x = 90°
   x = 45°.

   Hence ∠A = ∠C = 45°, and triangle ABC is a right isosceles triangle (right angle at B, other two angles 45° each).

3. Let AB = BC = s and let AC be the hypotenuse. By the Pythagorean theorem:
   AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = s^2 + s^2 = 2s^2.
   Therefore s^2 = AC^2 / 2 and s = AC / √2 = (AC · √2) / 2.

Final answer
- ∠A = ∠C = 45° (triangle ABC is a right isosceles triangle with ∠B = 90°).
- If AC denotes the hypotenuse, then AB = BC = AC / √2 = (AC · √2) / 2.

(No numerical lengths can be given because the diagram does not provide any side measures.)

Question  
Find the side and perimeter of a square whose diagonal is 10 cm.

Method  
Use the relation between diagonal d and side s of a square: d^2 = s^2 + s^2 = 2s^2 (Pythagoras in one of the right triangles formed by the diagonal). Solve for s, then compute the perimeter 4s.

Working
Let the side of the square be s cm and the diagonal be d = 10 cm.

d^2 = 2s^2  
⇒ 10^2 = 2s^2  
⇒ 100 = 2s^2  
⇒ s^2 = 100/2 = 50  
⇒ s = √50 = √(25·2) = 5√2 cm

Perimeter = 4s = 4 × 5√2 = 20√2 cm

(Approximate value: s ≈ 7.071 cm, perimeter ≈ 28.284 cm)

Final answer  
Side = 5√2 cm  
Perimeter = 20√2 cm (≈ 28.284 cm)

Question  
In the adjoining figure, ∠DFE = 90° and FG ⟂ ED. If GD = 8 and FG = 12, find  
i. EG  
ii. FD  
iii. EF

Method  
- Recognise triangle DEF is right-angled at F, and G is the foot of the perpendicular from F on hypotenuse ED.  
- Use the geometric mean (altitude) theorem: (FG)^2 = GD · GE.  
- Use Pythagoras in right triangles FGD and FGE to find FD and EF respectively.

Working
1. Find EG using the altitude (geometric mean) theorem
- FG^2 = GD · GE
- 12^2 = 8 · GE
- 144 = 8 · GE
- GE = 144 / 8 = 18

So EG = 18 units.

2. Find FD using triangle FGD (right-angled at G)
- FD^2 = FG^2 + GD^2
- FD^2 = 12^2 + 8^2 = 144 + 64 = 208
- FD = √208 = √(16·13) = 4√13

So FD = 4√13 units.

3. Find EF using triangle FGE (right-angled at G)
- EF^2 = FG^2 + GE^2
- EF^2 = 12^2 + 18^2 = 144 + 324 = 468
- EF = √468 = √(36·13) = 6√13

So EF = 6√13 units.

Final answer  
i. EG = 18 units  
ii. FD = 4√13 units  
iii. EF = 6√13 units

Question
Find the diagonal of a rectangle whose length is 35 cm and breadth is 12 cm.

Method
A rectangle has right angles at each corner. The diagonal divides the rectangle into a right-angled triangle whose legs are the length and breadth; the diagonal is the hypotenuse. Use the Pythagorean theorem: (hypotenuse)^2 = (leg1)^2 + (leg2)^2.

Diagram cue
A rectangle ABCD with right angle at B; diagonal AC is the hypotenuse of right triangle ABC. (No additional numerical information is taken from the diagram beyond the given side lengths.)

Working
Let ABCD be the rectangle with AB = 12 cm and BC = 35 cm. Consider right triangle ABC where AC is the diagonal (hypotenuse) and AB, BC are the legs.

By the Pythagorean theorem:
AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2
AC^2 = 12^2 + 35^2
AC^2 = 144 + 1225
AC^2 = 1369

So AC = sqrt(1369) = 37 cm.

Final answer
The diagonal of the rectangle is 37 cm.

Question 9

Given
- In triangle PQR, ∠PRQ = 90°.
- M is the midpoint of QR.

To prove
PQ^2 = 4·PM^2 − 3·PR^2.

Diagram cue
M lies on segment QR so RM = MQ and RM is collinear with QR; since PR ⟂ QR, PR is also perpendicular to RM.

Proof / Steps
1. Apply the Pythagorean theorem to right triangle PQR (right angle at R):
   PQ^2 = PR^2 + QR^2.            (1)

2. Since M is the midpoint of QR, QR = 2·RM. Substitute into (1):
   PQ^2 = PR^2 + (2·RM)^2 = PR^2 + 4·RM^2.    (2)

3. Apply the Pythagorean theorem to right triangle PRM (right angle at R):
   PM^2 = PR^2 + RM^2.              (3)

4. Solve (3) for RM^2:
   RM^2 = PM^2 − PR^2.              (4)

5. Substitute (4) into (2):
   PQ^2 = PR^2 + 4·(PM^2 − PR^2)
        = PR^2 + 4·PM^2 − 4·PR^2
        = 4·PM^2 − 3·PR^2.

Result
Hence PQ^2 = 4·PM^2 − 3·PR^2, as required.

Question  
Walls of two buildings on either side of a street are parallel to each other. A ladder 5.8 m long is placed on the street such that its top just reaches the window of a building at the height of 4 m. On turning the ladder over to the other side of the street, its top touches the window of the other building at a height 4.2 m. Find the width of the street.

Method  
Place the foot of the ladder at a point C on the road between the two walls. Let B and D be the points at the bases of the left and right walls respectively, so BD is the width of the street. When the ladder leans to the left, it forms a right triangle with vertical height AB = 4 m and horizontal distance BC; when leaned to the right, it forms a right triangle with vertical height DE = 4.2 m and horizontal distance CD = (BD − BC). Use the Pythagorean theorem in each position to find BC and CD, then add them to get BD.

Working
1. Let ladder length L = 5.8 m.
2. For the ladder leaning to the left:
   - AB = 4 m, BC = x (horizontal distance from left wall to foot C).
   - By Pythagoras: x^2 + 4^2 = 5.8^2.
   - Compute: 5.8^2 = 33.64 and 4^2 = 16.
   - So x^2 = 33.64 − 16 = 17.64, hence x = sqrt(17.64) = 4.2 m.
   - Thus BC = 4.2 m.

3. For the ladder leaning to the right:
   - DE = 4.2 m, CD = BD − BC = y (horizontal distance from foot C to right wall).
   - By Pythagoras: y^2 + 4.2^2 = 5.8^2.
   - Compute: 4.2^2 = 17.64 and 5.8^2 = 33.64.
   - So y^2 = 33.64 − 17.64 = 16, hence y = sqrt(16) = 4 m.
   - Thus CD = 4 m.

4. Width of the street BD = BC + CD = 4.2 + 4 = 8.2 m.

Final answer  
The width of the street is 8.2 metres.

Question  
Verify that (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (24, 25, 7) are Pythagorean triplets.

Method  
A triple of positive integers (a, b, c) is a Pythagorean triplet if the square of the largest number equals the sum of the squares of the other two; i.e. if c is largest, check c^2 = a^2 + b^2. For each given triple identify the largest number and verify this equality.

Working

i) (3, 4, 5)  
Largest number = 5.  
5^2 = 25.  
3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.  
Therefore 5^2 = 3^2 + 4^2.

ii) (5, 12, 13)  
Largest number = 13.  
13^2 = 169.  
5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169.  
Therefore 13^2 = 5^2 + 12^2.

iii) (8, 15, 17)  
Largest number = 17.  
17^2 = 289.  
8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289.  
Therefore 17^2 = 8^2 + 15^2.

iv) (24, 25, 7)  
Identify the largest number = 25.  
25^2 = 625.  
24^2 + 7^2 = 576 + 49 = 625.  
Therefore 25^2 = 24^2 + 7^2.

Final answer  
All four given triples satisfy the Pythagorean condition; hence each is a Pythagorean triplet.

Question  
Assign different values to a and b and obtain 5 Pythagorean triplets.

Method  
For any integers a and b with a > b > 0, the three numbers
- a^2 + b^2,  
- a^2 − b^2,  
- 2ab  
form a Pythagorean triplet because (a^2 − b^2)^2 + (2ab)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)^2.  
We will choose five different pairs (a, b), compute these three values, and list the triplets.

Working
1. Let a = 3, b = 2  
   a^2 + b^2 = 9 + 4 = 13  
   a^2 − b^2 = 9 − 4 = 5  
   2ab = 2 × 3 × 2 = 12  
   Triplet: (13, 5, 12)

2. Let a = 5, b = 4  
   a^2 + b^2 = 25 + 16 = 41  
   a^2 − b^2 = 25 − 16 = 9  
   2ab = 2 × 5 × 4 = 40  
   Triplet: (41, 9, 40)

3. Let a = 6, b = 1  
   a^2 + b^2 = 36 + 1 = 37  
   a^2 − b^2 = 36 − 1 = 35  
   2ab = 2 × 6 × 1 = 12  
   Triplet: (37, 35, 12)

4. Let a = 7, b = 2  
   a^2 + b^2 = 49 + 4 = 53  
   a^2 − b^2 = 49 − 4 = 45  
   2ab = 2 × 7 × 2 = 28  
   Triplet: (53, 45, 28)

5. Let a = 8, b = 3  
   a^2 + b^2 = 64 + 9 = 73  
   a^2 − b^2 = 64 − 9 = 55  
   2ab = 2 × 8 × 3 = 48  
   Triplet: (73, 55, 48)

Final answer  
Five Pythagorean triplets obtained are:
- (13, 5, 12)  
- (41, 9, 40)  
- (37, 35, 12)  
- (53, 45, 28)  
- (73, 55, 48)

Note: In each triplet the numbers can be written in any order; usually the largest is taken as the hypotenuse.

 Solution:

 In ∆PQR, point S is the midpoint of side QR. [Given]

 ∴ seg PS is the median.

 ∴ PQ 2 + PR 2 = 2 PS 2 + 2 SR 2 [Apollonius theorem]

 ∴ 11 2 + 17 2 = 2 (13)2 + 2 SR 2

 ∴ 121 + 289 = 2 (169)+ 2 SR 2

 ∴ 410 = 338+ 2 SR 2

 ∴ 2 SR 2 = 410 – 338

 ∴ 2 SR 2 = 72

 ∴ SR 2 = 72 2 = 36

 ∴ SR = 36−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = 6 units Now, QR = 2 SR [S is the midpoint of QR]

 = 2 × 6

Question 2.

 In ∆ABC, AB = 10, AC = 7, BC = 9, then find the length of the median drawn from point C to side AB.

 ∴ 130 = 2 CD 2 + 50

 ∴ 2 CD 2 = 130 – 50

 ∴ 2 CD 2 = 80

 ∴ CD 2 = 80 2 = 40

Question  
In triangle PQR, S is the midpoint of side QR. If PQ = 11, PR = 17, PS = 13, find QR.

Method  
Use Apollonius' theorem: for a triangle, the sum of the squares of two sides equals twice the sum of the square of the median to the third side and the square of half that third side. Here that gives a relation between PQ, PR, PS and SR (where SR = half of QR).

Working
- By Apollonius' theorem (with PS the median to QR):
  PQ^2 + PR^2 = 2(PS^2 + SR^2).

- Substitute the given values:
  11^2 + 17^2 = 2(13^2 + SR^2).

- Compute the squares:
  121 + 289 = 2(169 + SR^2)
  410 = 338 + 2 SR^2

- Solve for SR^2:
  2 SR^2 = 410 − 338 = 72
  SR^2 = 36
  SR = 6 (taking the positive length)

- Since S is the midpoint, QR = 2 · SR = 2 · 6 = 12.

Final answer  
QR = 12 units.

Question  
In ∆ABC, AB = 10, AC = 7, BC = 9. Find the length of the median drawn from point C to side AB.

Method  
Let CD be the median from C to AB, so D is the midpoint of AB. Hence BD = AD = AB/2. Use Apollonius' theorem for the median:  
AC^2 + BC^2 = 2(CD^2 + (AB/2)^2).  
Solve this equation for CD.

Diagram cue  
If a diagram is shown, it only confirms D is the midpoint of AB; no other diagram measurements are used.

Working
1. BD = AB/2 = 10/2 = 5.  
2. Apply Apollonius' theorem:
   AC^2 + BC^2 = 2(CD^2 + (AB/2)^2).
3. Substitute the given lengths:
   7^2 + 9^2 = 2(CD^2 + 5^2)
   ⇒ 49 + 81 = 2(CD^2 + 25)
   ⇒ 130 = 2CD^2 + 50.
4. Solve for CD^2:
   2CD^2 = 130 − 50 = 80
   ⇒ CD^2 = 40.
5. Take square root:
   CD = √40 = √(4·10) = 2√10 units.

Final answer  
The length of the median from C to AB is 2√10 units.

Question
In the adjoining figure, PS is the median of QR (so S is midpoint of QR) and PT ⟂ QR. Prove that
i. PR^2 = PS^2 + QR·ST + (QR/2)^2
ii. PQ^2 = PS^2 − QR·ST + (QR/2)^2

Diagram cue: the diagram shows QR as a straight line, S its midpoint, PT perpendicular to QR and meeting QR at T. We place QR on a horizontal axis and use coordinates to compute the required squares of lengths (no other numerical values from the diagram are assumed).

Method
Place QR on the x-axis with S at the origin. Let QR = 2d, so QS = SR = d. Let T have x-coordinate t (so ST = t), and let PT = h (so P has coordinates (t, h)). Express PS^2, PR^2 and PQ^2 in these coordinates and simplify using QR = 2d.

Working
1. Set-up
- Let d = QR/2.
- Put S at (0,0). Then choose R at (−d, 0) and Q at (+d, 0).
- Let T be at (t, 0); then ST = t.
- Since PT ⟂ QR, point P has coordinates (t, h) with PT = h.

2. PS^2
PS^2 = (t − 0)^2 + (h − 0)^2 = t^2 + h^2.

3. PR^2
PR^2 = distance^2 between P(t,h) and R(−d,0)
= (t − (−d))^2 + (h − 0)^2
= (t + d)^2 + h^2
= t^2 + 2dt + d^2 + h^2
= (t^2 + h^2) + 2dt + d^2
= PS^2 + 2d·t + d^2.

Since QR = 2d and ST = t, 2d·t = QR·ST and d^2 = (QR/2)^2. Thus
PR^2 = PS^2 + QR·ST + (QR/2)^2.  (This proves (i).)

4. PQ^2
PQ^2 = distance^2 between P(t,h) and Q(d,0)
= (t − d)^2 + h^2
= t^2 − 2dt + d^2 + h^2
= (t^2 + h^2) − 2d·t + d^2
= PS^2 − 2d·t + d^2.

Again 2d·t = QR·ST and d^2 = (QR/2)^2, so
PQ^2 = PS^2 − QR·ST + (QR/2)^2.  (This proves (ii).)

Final answer
i. PR^2 = PS^2 + QR·ST + (QR/2)^2
ii. PQ^2 = PS^2 − QR·ST + (QR/2)^2

Question  
In ∆ABC, point M is the midpoint of side BC. If AB^2 + AC^2 = 290 cm^2 and AM = 8 cm, find BC.

Diagram cue: A diagram is supplied in the textbook, but it gives no additional numerical values beyond those stated in the problem.

Method  
Use Apollonius' theorem for the median AM: for M the midpoint of BC,
AB^2 + AC^2 = 2(AM^2 + BM^2),
and BM = MC = (1/2)BC. Solve this equation for BM, then double to get BC.

Working
1. Apply Apollonius' theorem:
   AB^2 + AC^2 = 2(AM^2 + BM^2).

2. Substitute the given values AB^2 + AC^2 = 290 and AM = 8:
   290 = 2(8^2 + BM^2).

3. Evaluate 8^2 = 64:
   290 = 2(64 + BM^2).

4. Divide both sides by 2:
   145 = 64 + BM^2.

5. Solve for BM^2:
   BM^2 = 145 − 64 = 81.

6. Take positive square root (lengths are positive):
   BM = 9 cm.

7. BC = 2 × BM = 2 × 9 = 18 cm.

Final answer  
BC = 18 cm.

Question
In the adjoining figure, point T is in the interior of rectangle PQRS. Prove that TS^2 + TQ^2 = TP^2 + TR^2.

Method
Use coordinates: place the rectangle on a Cartesian plane so vertices have simple coordinates, put T at (x,y) with 0 < x < a and 0 < y < b, and apply the distance formula to compute the four squared distances and compare the sums.

Working
1. Place the rectangle PQRS with
   - P = (0, 0)
   - Q = (a, 0)
   - R = (a, b)
   - S = (0, b)
   where a > 0 and b > 0.  
   Let T = (x, y) be a point in the interior, so 0 < x < a and 0 < y < b.

2. Compute squared distances from T to the four vertices using the distance formula:
   - TP^2 = (x − 0)^2 + (y − 0)^2 = x^2 + y^2.
   - TQ^2 = (x − a)^2 + (y − 0)^2 = (x − a)^2 + y^2.
   - TR^2 = (x − a)^2 + (y − b)^2.
   - TS^2 = (x − 0)^2 + (y − b)^2 = x^2 + (y − b)^2.

3. Form the two sums:
   - TS^2 + TQ^2 = [x^2 + (y − b)^2] + [(x − a)^2 + y^2]
                 = x^2 + (x − a)^2 + y^2 + (y − b)^2.
   - TP^2 + TR^2 = [x^2 + y^2] + [(x − a)^2 + (y − b)^2]
                 = x^2 + (x − a)^2 + y^2 + (y − b)^2.

4. The two expressions are identical, hence
   TS^2 + TQ^2 = TP^2 + TR^2.

Final answer
TS^2 + TQ^2 = TP^2 + TR^2, as required.

Question 1

In ∆ABC, ∠C is an acute angle and AD ⟂ BC (D lies on BC). Prove that AB² = BC² + AC² − 2·BC·DC.

Given
- ∠C is acute.
- AD ⟂ BC and D lies on BC (so B–D–C are collinear).

To prove
AB² = BC² + AC² − 2 · BC · DC

Proof/Steps
1. Introduce notation for lengths:
   - Let AB = c, AC = b, BC = a, DC = x, AD = p.
   - Since D lies on BC with B–D–C, BD = BC − DC = a − x. (Diagram cue: D is between B and C, so BD + DC = BC.)

2. Apply Pythagoras in right triangle ABD (∠ADB = 90°):
   AB² = AD² + BD²
   ⇒ c² = p² + (a − x)²
   ⇒ c² = p² + (a² − 2ax + x²).    (1)

3. Apply Pythagoras in right triangle ADC (∠ADC = 90°):
   AC² = AD² + DC²
   ⇒ b² = p² + x²
   ⇒ p² = b² − x².                 (2)

4. Substitute p² from (2) into (1):
   c² = (b² − x²) + (a² − 2ax + x²)
   The x² terms cancel:
   c² = a² + b² − 2ax.

5. Replace symbols by original segment names:
   AB² = BC² + AC² − 2 · BC · DC.

Result
Hence AB² = BC² + AC² − 2·BC·DC, as required.

Question 2

Given
- In triangle ABC, ∠ACB is obtuse.
- AD ⟂ BC, where D is the foot of the perpendicular from A to the line BC.

Diagram cue
- Because ∠ACB is obtuse, the perpendicular from A meets the line BC at a point D lying on the extension of BC beyond C. Thus B, C, D are collinear with C between B and D; so BD = BC + CD.

To prove
AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 + 2 · BC · CD

Proof / Steps
1. Introduce notation:
   - Let AB = c, AC = b, BC = a, CD = x, AD = h.

2. Consider right triangle ADB (since AD ⟂ BC):
   AB^2 = AD^2 + BD^2
   ⇒ c^2 = h^2 + BD^2.
   Using BD = BC + CD = a + x,
   c^2 = h^2 + (a + x)^2
   = h^2 + a^2 + 2ax + x^2.   (1)

3. Consider right triangle ADC:
   AC^2 = AD^2 + DC^2
   ⇒ b^2 = h^2 + x^2
   ⇒ h^2 = b^2 − x^2.         (2)

4. Substitute (2) into (1):
   c^2 = (b^2 − x^2) + a^2 + 2ax + x^2
   = a^2 + b^2 + 2ax.

5. Replace a and x by the original segment names:
   AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 + 2 · BC · CD.

Result
AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 + 2 · BC · CD.

Question 3

Given:
- In triangle ABC, M is the midpoint of BC.
- AM ⟂ BC.

To prove:
AB^2 + AC^2 = 2·AM^2 + 2·BM^2

Proof/Steps:
1. Because AM is perpendicular to BC, angles AMB and AMC are right angles. Thus triangles ABM and ACM are right-angled at M.

2. Apply the Pythagorean theorem to triangle ABM:
   AB^2 = AM^2 + BM^2.        (1)

3. Apply the Pythagorean theorem to triangle ACM:
   AC^2 = AM^2 + CM^2.        (2)

4. Add equations (1) and (2):
   AB^2 + AC^2 = (AM^2 + BM^2) + (AM^2 + CM^2)
               = 2·AM^2 + (BM^2 + CM^2).

5. Since M is the midpoint of BC, BM = CM. Therefore BM^2 = CM^2 and BM^2 + CM^2 = 2·BM^2.

6. Substitute into the sum:
   AB^2 + AC^2 = 2·AM^2 + 2·BM^2.

Result:
AB^2 + AC^2 = 2·AM^2 + 2·BM^2.  (Proved)

Question 2.

 Solve the following examples.

 i. Find the height of an equilateral triangle having side 2a.

 ii. Do sides 7 cm, 24 cm, 25 cm form a right angled triangle? Give reason.

 iii. Find the length of a diagonal of a rectangle having sides 11 cm and 60 cm.

 iv. Find the length of the hypotenuse of a right angled triangle if remaining sides are 9 cm and 12 cm.

 v. A side of an isosceles right angled triangle is x. Find its hypotenuse.

 vi. In ∆PQR, PQ = 8–√, QR = 5–√, PR = 3–√ . Is ∆PQR a right angled triangle? If yes, which angle is of 90°?

 Solution:

 i. Let ∆ABC be the given equilateral triangle.

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-7.png?resize=123%2C134&ssl=1)

 ∴ ∠B = 60° [Angle of an equilateral triangle]

 Let AD ⊥BC, B – D – C.

 In ∆ABD, ∠B = 60°, ∠ADB = 90°

 ∴ ∠BAD = 30° [Remaining angle of a triangle]

 ∴ ∆ABD is a 30° – 60° – 90° triangle.

 ∴ AD = 3√2 AB [Side opposite to 60°]

 = 3√2 × 2a

 = a 3–√ units

 The height of the equilateral triangle is a 3–√ units.

ii. The sides of the triangle are 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm.

 The longest side of the triangle is 25 cm.

 ∴ (25)2 = 625

 Now, sum of the squares of the remaining sides is,

 (7)2 + (24)2 = 49 + 576

 = 625

 ∴ (25)2 = (7)2 + (24)2

 ∴ Square of the longest side is equal to the sum of the squares of the remaining two sides.

 ∴ The given sides will form a right angled triangle. [Converse of Pythagoras theorem]

iii. Let ꠸ABCD be the given rectangle.

 AB = 11 cm, BC = 60 cm

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-1.jpg?resize=132%2C144&ssl=1)

 In ∆ABC, ∠B = 90° [Angle of a rectangle]

 ∴ AC 2 = AB 2 + BC 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 = 112 + 602

 = 121 +3600

 = 3721

 ∴ AC = 3721−−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = 61 cm

 The length of the diagonal of the rectangle is 61 cm.

 ∴ The length of the diagonal of the rectangle is 61 cm.

iv. Let ∆PQR be the given right angled triangle.

 In ∆PQR, ∠Q = 90°

![Image 11: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-26.jpg?resize=202%2C130&ssl=1)

 ∴ PR 2 = PQ 2 + QR 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 = 9 2 + 12 2

 = 81 + 144

 = 225

 ∴ PR = 225−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = 15 cm

 ∴ The length of the hypotenuse of the right angled triangle is 15 cm.

v. Let ∆PQR be the given right angled isosceles triangle.

 PQ = QR = x.

![Image 12: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-27.jpg?resize=148%2C142&ssl=1)

 In ∆PQR, ∠Q = 90° [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ PR 2 = PQ 2 + QR 2

 = x 2 + x 2

 = 2x 2

 ∴ PR = 2 x 2−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = x 2–√ units

 ∴ The hypotenuse of the right angled isosceles triangle is x 2–√ units.

 ∴ The hypotenuse of the right angled isosceles triangle is x 2–√ units.

vi. Longest side of ∆PQR = PQ = 8–√

 ∴ PQ 2 = (8–√)2 = 8

 Now, sum of the squares of the remaining sides is,

![Image 13: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-28.jpg?resize=221%2C144&ssl=1)

 QR 2 + PR 2 = (5–√)2 + (3–√)2

 = 5 + 3

 = 8

 ∴ PQ 2 = QR 2 + PR 2

 ∴ Square of the longest side is equal to the sum of the squares of the remaining two sides.

 ∴ ∆PQR is a right angled triangle. [Converse of Pythagoras theorem]

 Now, PQ is the hypotenuse.

 ∴∠PRQ = 90° [Angle opposite to hypotenuse]

 ∴ ∆PQR is a right angled triangle in which ∠PRQ is of 90°.

Question 3.

 In ∆RST, ∠S = 90°, ∠T = 30°, RT = 12 cm, then find RS and ST.

 Solution:

 in ∆RST, ∠S = 900, ∠T = 30° [Given]

 ∴ ∠R = 60° [Remaining angle of a triangle]

 ∴ ∆RST is a 30° – 60° – 90° triangle.

![Image 14: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-29.jpg?resize=166%2C139&ssl=1)

 ∴ RS = 1 2 RT [Side opposite to 30°]

 = 1 2 × 12 = 6cm

 Also, ST = 3√2 RT [Side opposite to 60°]

 = 3√2 × 12 = 6 3–√ cm

 ∴ RS = 6 cm and ST = 6 3–√ cm

Question 4.

 Find the diagonal of a rectangle whose length is 16 cm and area is 192 sq. cm.

 Solution:

 Let ꠸ABCD be the given rectangle.

 BC = 16cm

 Area of rectangle = length × breadth

 Area of ꠸ABCD = BC × AB

![Image 15: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-30.jpg?resize=172%2C114&ssl=1)

 ∴ 192 = I6 × AB

 ∴ AB = 192 16

 = 12cm

 Now, in ∆ABC, ∠B = 90° [Angle of a rectangle]

 ∴ AC 2 = AB 2 + BC 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 = 122 + 162

 = 144 + 256

 =400

 ∴ AC = 400−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = 20cm

 ∴ The diagonal of the rectangle is 20 cm.

Question 5.

 Find the length of the side and perimeter of an equilateral triangle whose height is 3–√ cm.

 Solution:

 Let ∆ABC be the given equilateral triangle.

 ∴ ∠B = 60° [Angle of an equilateral triangle]

![Image 16: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 2 Pythagoras Theorem Problem Set 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-2-Pythagoras-Theorem-Problem-Set-2-31.jpg?resize=144%2C132&ssl=1)

 AD ⊥ BC, B – D – C.

 In ∆ABD, ∠B =60°, ∠ADB = 90°

 ∴ ∠BAD = 30° [Remaining angle of a triangle]

 ∴ ∆ABD is a 30° – 60° – 90° triangle.

 ∴ AD = 3√2 AB [Side opposite to 600]

 ∴ 3–√ = 3√2 AB

 ∴ AB = 2 3√3√

 ∴ AB = 2cm

 ∴ Side of equilateral triangle = 2cm

 Perimeter of ∆ABC = 3 × side

 = 3 × AB

 = 3 × 2

 = 6cm

 ∴ The length of the side and perimeter of the equilateral triangle are 2 cm and 6 cm respectively.

Question 6.

 In ∆ABC, seg AP is a median. If BC = 18, AB2 + AC2 = 260, find AP.

 Solution:

 PC = 1 2 BC [P is the midpoint of side BC]

Question  
Some multiple-choice items on Pythagoras theorem. Select the correct alternative and show working.

i. Out of the following which is the Pythagorean triplet?  
(A) (1,5,10)  (B) (3,4,5)  (C) (2,2,2)  (D) (5,5,2)

Method  
A triple (a, b, c) is Pythagorean if a^2 + b^2 = c^2 for some ordering with c the largest.

Working  
Check (3,4,5): 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2.  
(1,5,10): 1 + 25 = 26 ≠ 100.  
(2,2,2): 4 + 4 = 8 ≠ 4.  
(5,5,2): 25 + 25 = 50 ≠ 4.

Final answer: (B) (3,4,5)

---

ii. In a right angled triangle, if sum of the squares of the sides making right angle is 169, then what is the length of the hypotenuse?  
(A) 15  (B) 13  (C) 5  (D) 12

Method  
For a right triangle with legs of lengths a and b and hypotenuse c, a^2 + b^2 = c^2. If a^2 + b^2 is given, take square root to find c.

Working  
Given a^2 + b^2 = 169, so c^2 = 169 ⇒ c = √169 = 13.

Final answer: (B) 13

---

iii. Out of the dates given below which date constitutes a Pythagorean triplet?  
(A) 15/08/17  (B) 16/08/16  (C) 3/5/17  (D) 4/9/15

Method  
Treat the three numbers in each date as the triple (day, month, year) and check whether the squares of the two smaller add to the square of the largest.

Working  
For 15/08/17 → 15^2 + 8^2 = 225 + 64 = 289 = 17^2.  
Other choices do not satisfy the relation (for example 16,8,16 gives 256+64=320 ≠ 256).

Final answer: (A) 15/08/17

---

iv. If a, b, c are sides of a triangle and a^2 + b^2 = c^2, name the type of the triangle.  
(A) Obtuse angled triangle  (B) Acute angled triangle  (C) Right angled triangle  (D) Equilateral triangle

Method  
By converse of Pythagoras: if for three sides a^2 + b^2 = c^2 (with c largest) the triangle is right-angled at the vertex between sides a and b.

Final answer: (C) Right angled triangle

---

v. Find perimeter of a square if its diagonal is 10√2 cm.  
(A) 10 cm  (B) 40√2 cm  (C) 20 cm  (D) 40 cm

Method  
For a square of side s, diagonal d = s√2. Solve s from d, then perimeter = 4s.

Working  
Given d = 10√2, so s√2 = 10√2 ⇒ s = 10. Perimeter = 4s = 4 × 10 = 40 cm.

Final answer: (D) 40 cm

---

vi. Altitude on the hypotenuse of a right angled triangle divides it in two parts of lengths 4 cm and 9 cm. Find the length of the altitude.

In triangle ABC, AB = 6√3 cm, AC = 12 cm, BC = 6 cm. Find measure of ∠A.

Method

AC^2 = 12^2 = 144,
BC^2 = 6^2 = 36.

cos A = (108 + 144 − 36) / (2 · 6√3 · 12)
= (216) / (144√3)
Simplify:

Thus cos A = √3/2, so ∠A = 30°.

Question 2

Solve the following examples.

i. Find the height of an equilateral triangle having side 2a.
ii. Do sides 7 cm, 24 cm, 25 cm form a right angled triangle? Give reason.
iii. Find the length of a diagonal of a rectangle having sides 11 cm and 60 cm.
iv. Find the length of the hypotenuse of a right angled triangle if remaining sides are 9 cm and 12 cm.
v. A side of an isosceles right angled triangle is x. Find its hypotenuse.
vi. In ∆PQR, PQ = √8, QR = √5, PR = √3. Is ∆PQR a right angled triangle? If yes, which angle is 90°?

---

i. Height of an equilateral triangle of side 2a

Method
- Drop an altitude from one vertex to the opposite side; it bisects the base and makes two congruent right triangles.
- Use Pythagoras on one right triangle.

Working
- Base half = (2a)/2 = a.
- Height h satisfies h^2 + a^2 = (2a)^2 = 4a^2.
- So h^2 = 4a^2 − a^2 = 3a^2, hence h = a√3.

Final answer
- Height = a√3.

---

ii. Do sides 7 cm, 24 cm, 25 cm form a right angled triangle?

Method
- Check the converse of Pythagoras: if square of largest side = sum of squares of other two, triangle is right-angled.

Working
- Largest side = 25. 25^2 = 625.
- 7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625.

Final answer
- Yes. Since 25^2 = 7^2 + 24^2, the three lengths form a right triangle (hypotenuse = 25 cm).

---

iii. Diagonal of rectangle with sides 11 cm and 60 cm

Method
- Diagonal d of rectangle: d^2 = side1^2 + side2^2 (right triangle formed by sides and diagonal).

Working
- d^2 = 11^2 + 60^2 = 121 + 3600 = 3721.
- d = √3721 = 61.

Final answer
- Diagonal = 61 cm.

---

iv. Hypotenuse when other sides are 9 cm and 12 cm

Method
- If the given sides are the two legs of a right triangle, hypotenuse c = √(9^2 + 12^2).

Working
- c^2 = 9^2 + 12^2 = 81 + 144 = 225 → c = √225 = 15.

Final answer
- Hypotenuse = 15 cm.

---

v. Isosceles right-angled triangle with a side x — find hypotenuse

Method
- In an isosceles right triangle the two equal sides (legs) meet at 90°. Hypotenuse = leg × √2.
- (If instead x were the hypotenuse, the equal legs would each be x/√2. Clarify which is meant.)

Working
- Assuming x is the length of each equal leg: hypotenuse = x√2.

Final answer
- If x is a leg, hypotenuse = x√2.
- (If x is the hypotenuse, each leg = x/√2.)

---

vi. Determine whether ∆PQR with PQ = √8, QR = √5, PR = √3 is right angled; identify the right angle

Method
- Compare squares: if the square of the longest side equals the sum of squares of the other two sides, the triangle is right angled; the right angle is at the vertex opposite the longest side.

Working
- Compute squares: PQ^2 = 8, QR^2 = 5, PR^2 = 3.
- Longest side is PQ (√8 ≈ 2.828 > √5 ≈ 2.236 and √3 ≈ 1.732).
- Check: QR^2 + PR^2 = 5 + 3 = 8 = PQ^2.

Final answer
- Yes. ∆PQR is right angled; the right angle is at vertex R (side PQ is the hypotenuse, so ∠R = 90°).

Let ∆PQR be a right-angled isosceles triangle with PQ = QR = x. Find the length of the hypotenuse PR.

Method
Use the Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, (hypotenuse)^2 = (sum of squares of the other two sides).

PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2
      = x^2 + x^2
      = 2x^2.

Question (vi)
In ∆PQR the side lengths are PQ = √8, QR = √5 and PR = √3. Show that ∆PQR is a right-angled triangle and state which angle is 90°.

Method
Use the converse of the Pythagorean theorem: if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, the triangle is right-angled and the longest side is the hypotenuse.

Diagram cue: The triangle with the three given side lengths is provided; those lengths alone determine the verification.

Working
Compute squares of the given sides:
PQ^2 = (√8)^2 = 8,
QR^2 = (√5)^2 = 5,
PR^2 = (√3)^2 = 3.

Identify the longest side: PQ^2 = 8 is the largest, so PQ is the longest side and candidate hypotenuse.

Check the converse condition:
QR^2 + PR^2 = 5 + 3 = 8 = PQ^2.

Since PQ^2 = QR^2 + PR^2, by the converse of Pythagoras, ∆PQR is a right-angled triangle and PQ is the hypotenuse. The angle opposite PQ is ∠PRQ (the angle at vertex R), so that angle is 90°.

Final answer
∆PQR is right-angled with ∠PRQ = 90° (PQ is the hypotenuse).

Method

  ST = (hypotenuse · √3)/2 = (12 · √3)/2 = 6√3 cm.

RS = 6 cm and ST = 6√3 cm.

Question  
In triangle ABC, AP is a median. If BC = 18 and AB^2 + AC^2 = 260, find the length of AP.

Method  
Use Apollonius' theorem for a median: in any triangle ABC with median AP (P midpoint of BC),
AB^2 + AC^2 = 2[AP^2 + PC^2].
Since P is midpoint of BC, PC = BC/2. Substitute and solve for AP.

Working
1. Compute PC:
   PC = BC/2 = 18/2 = 9.

2. Apply Apollonius' theorem:
   AB^2 + AC^2 = 2[AP^2 + PC^2]
   Given AB^2 + AC^2 = 260, so
   260 = 2[AP^2 + 9^2] = 2[AP^2 + 81].

3. Divide both sides by 2:
   130 = AP^2 + 81.

4. Solve for AP^2:
   AP^2 = 130 − 81 = 49.

5. Take the positive square root (lengths are positive):
   AP = √49 = 7 (units).

Final answer  
AP = 7 units.

Question  
∆ABC is an equilateral triangle. Point P is on base BC such that PC = (1/3) BC. If AB = 6 cm, find AP.

Method  
1. Draw AD ⟂ BC with D on BC (altitude from A). In an equilateral triangle the altitude is also a median, so D is the midpoint of BC.  
2. Compute PC and CD, then DP = CD − PC.  
3. Use right triangle ΔADP (right at D) and Pythagoras to find AP.

Working
- Since ΔABC is equilateral with side AB = 6 cm, all sides equal:
  BC = 6 cm.

- PC = (1/3) BC = (1/3) × 6 = 2 cm.

- D is midpoint of BC, so
  CD = (1/2) BC = (1/2) × 6 = 3 cm.

- Therefore DP = CD − PC = 3 − 2 = 1 cm.

- Altitude AD of an equilateral triangle of side 6:
  AD = (√3 / 2) × 6 = 3√3 cm.

- In right triangle ΔADP (right angle at D),
  AP^2 = AD^2 + DP^2
       = (3√3)^2 + 1^2
       = 27 + 1
       = 28.

- So AP = √28 = 2√7 cm.

Final answer  
AP = 2√7 cm.

Question  
Prove that in parallelogram ABCD with diagonals AC and BD meeting at M,
AC^2 + BD^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + AD^2.

Method  
1. Use the fact that in a parallelogram diagonals bisect each other, so M is the midpoint of both AC and BD.  
2. Apply Apollonius' theorem to triangle ABC with BM as the median to side AC.  
3. Substitute AM = AC/2 and BM = BD/2, use equal opposite sides AB = CD and BC = AD, and simplify.

Working
Given: ABCD is a parallelogram, diagonals AC and BD intersect at M.
Then M is the midpoint of AC and of BD, so
AM = MC = AC/2 and BM = MD = BD/2.    (1)

In triangle ABC, BM is the median to AC. Apollonius' theorem states:
AB^2 + BC^2 = 2(BM^2 + AM^2).    (2)

Substitute the midpoint values from (1) into (2):
AB^2 + BC^2 = 2((BD/2)^2 + (AC/2)^2)
             = 2(BD^2/4 + AC^2/4)
             = (BD^2 + AC^2)/2.

Multiply both sides by 2:
2AB^2 + 2BC^2 = AC^2 + BD^2.    (3)

Because ABCD is a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal:
AB = CD and BC = AD. Replace one copy of AB^2 by CD^2 and one copy of BC^2 by AD^2 in (3):
AB^2 + CD^2 + BC^2 + AD^2 = AC^2 + BD^2.

Reordering gives the required result:
AC^2 + BD^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + AD^2.

Final answer  
AC^2 + BD^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + AD^2, as required.

Question  
Pranali and Prasad start walking from the same point; Pranali goes East and Prasad goes North. They walk at the same constant speed. After 2 hours the distance between them is 15√2 km. Find their speed (in km/h).

Method  
- The paths are at right angles, so the line joining their positions after 2 hours is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the distances each person walked.  
- Let each leg (distance walked by each person in 2 hours) be d km. Use the Pythagorean theorem to relate d and the given hypotenuse.  
- Find d, then speed = distance / time = d / 2.

Working  
1. Let d be the distance each person walked in 2 hours. Then the separation after 2 hours is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs d and d.  
2. By Pythagoras: (hypotenuse)^2 = d^2 + d^2 = 2d^2.  
   Given hypotenuse = 15√2 km, so  
   (15√2)^2 = 2d^2.  
3. Compute left side: (15√2)^2 = 15^2 × (√2)^2 = 225 × 2 = 450.  
   Thus 450 = 2d^2 ⇒ d^2 = 225 ⇒ d = 15 km (taking positive distance).  
4. Each walked d = 15 km in 2 hours. Speed = distance / time = 15 / 2 = 7.5 km/h.

Final answer  
The speed of both Pranali and Prasad is 7.5 km/h.

Question 11

Given
- In triangle ABC, ∠BAC = 90°.
- BL is a median, so L is midpoint of AC.
- CM is a median, so M is midpoint of AB.

To prove
4 (BL^2 + CM^2) = 5 BC^2

Proof / Steps
1. Because L lies on AC, AL is collinear with AC. Since ∠BAC = 90°, the angle between BA and AL is 90°. Hence triangle BAL is right-angled at A. By the Pythagorean theorem,
   BL^2 = BA^2 + AL^2.            (1)

2. Similarly, M lies on AB, so AM is collinear with AB. Triangle CAM is right-angled at A, so
   CM^2 = CA^2 + AM^2.            (2)

3. Add (1) and (2):
   BL^2 + CM^2 = (BA^2 + CA^2) + (AL^2 + AM^2).    (3)

4. Since L and M are midpoints,
   AL = AC/2  and  AM = AB/2.
   Therefore AL^2 + AM^2 = (AC^2)/4 + (AB^2)/4 = (1/4)(AB^2 + AC^2).   (4)

5. Substitute (4) into (3):
   BL^2 + CM^2 = (AB^2 + AC^2) + (1/4)(AB^2 + AC^2)
                = (5/4)(AB^2 + AC^2).                        (5)

6. Multiply both sides of (5) by 4:
   4(BL^2 + CM^2) = 5(AB^2 + AC^2).                        (6)

7. Finally, since triangle ABC is right-angled at A, Pythagoras gives
   BC^2 = AB^2 + AC^2.                                       (7)

8. Replace AB^2 + AC^2 in (6) by BC^2 using (7):
   4(BL^2 + CM^2) = 5 BC^2.

Result
Hence proved: 4 (BL^2 + CM^2) = 5 BC^2.

Question  
Sum of the squares of two adjacent sides of a parallelogram is 130 cm² and one diagonal has length 14 cm. Find the length of the other diagonal.

Method  
Use the identity for a parallelogram: the sum of the squares of its two diagonals equals twice the sum of the squares of two adjacent sides. (A quick derivation: represent adjacent side vectors by a and b; then diagonals are a + b and b − a. Compute |a+b|² + |b−a|² = 2(|a|² + |b|²).)

Working
- Given AB² + AD² = 130 and BD = 14 cm.
- By the parallelogram identity: AC² + BD² = 2(AB² + AD²).
- Substitute values: AC² + 14² = 2 × 130 = 260.
- So AC² + 196 = 260 ⇒ AC² = 260 − 196 = 64.
- Therefore AC = √64 = 8 cm.

Final answer  
The length of the other diagonal AC is 8 cm.

   From (2): AD^2 = AC^2 − x^2.                              (3)

4. Substitute (3) into (1):
   AB^2 = (AC^2 − x^2) + 9x^2 = AC^2 + 8x^2.                 (4)

5. Replace x by BC/4: x^2 = (BC^2)/16. Thus from (4),
   AB^2 = AC^2 + 8 · (BC^2/16) = AC^2 + (BC^2)/2.

6. Multiply both sides by 2:
   2AB^2 = 2AC^2 + BC^2.

Final answer  
Hence proved: 2 AB^2 = 2 AC^2 + BC^2.

Question  
In isosceles triangle ABC, AB = AC = 13 cm and BC = 10 cm. Let G be the centroid. Find AG (distance from vertex A to the centroid).

Method  
1. Let D be the midpoint of BC (so AD is the median from A).  
2. Use the right triangle formed by AB, AD, and BD (in an isosceles triangle the median from the apex is also an altitude) to find AD.  
3. Use the property that the centroid divides a median in the ratio 2:1 (vertex to centroid : centroid to midpoint) to get AG = (2/3)·AD.

Working
- Since D is midpoint of BC, BD = CD = BC/2 = 10/2 = 5 cm.
- In right triangle ABD (AB is hypotenuse because AD is altitude in this isosceles triangle),
  AB^2 = AD^2 + BD^2.
  So 13^2 = AD^2 + 5^2.
  169 = AD^2 + 25.
  AD^2 = 169 − 25 = 144.
  AD = √144 = 12 cm.
- The centroid G divides AD in the ratio AG : GD = 2 : 1, so AG = (2/3)·AD = (2/3)·12 = 8 cm.

Final answer  
AG = 8 cm.

Question
In trapezium ABCD, AB ∥ DC, BD ⟂ AD and AC ⟂ BC. If AD = 15, BC = 15 and AB = 25, find area of ABCD.

Method
1. Put AB on the x-axis with A at (0,0) and B at (25,0). This makes perpendiculars to AB vertical lines.
2. Use right triangle ACB (AC ⟂ BC) to find AC, then compute the perpendicular distance CF from C to AB and the x-coordinate of F.
3. Since DC ∥ AB, D and C have the same y-coordinate; use AD = 15 to find the x-coordinate of D and then DC.
4. Compute area of trapezium using area = (1/2)·(sum of parallel sides)·(distance between them).

Working
1. In right triangle ACB, AC ⟂ BC, so by Pythagoras:
   AB^2 = AC^2 + BC^2.
   25^2 = AC^2 + 15^2
   625 = AC^2 + 225
   AC^2 = 400 ⇒ AC = 20.

2. Area of triangle ABC = (1/2)·AC·BC = (1/2)·20·15 = 150.
   This area is also (1/2)·AB·(distance from C to AB) = (1/2)·25·CF.
   So 150 = (1/2)·25·CF ⇒ CF = (150·2)/25 = 12.

   Place AB on x-axis: A(0,0), B(25,0). Since CF is vertical and FB is along AB:
   FB = distance from F to B = 25 − x_F. Also in right triangle CFB:
   BC^2 = CF^2 + FB^2 ⇒ 15^2 = 12^2 + FB^2
   225 = 144 + FB^2 ⇒ FB^2 = 81 ⇒ FB = 9.
   Thus F has x-coordinate x_F = 25 − 9 = 16, and C is at (16,12).

3. DC ∥ AB, so DC is horizontal; therefore D has same y-coordinate as C, i.e. y = 12. Let D = (x_D, 12).
   Given AD = 15, with A(0,0):
   AD^2 = x_D^2 + 12^2 = 15^2 ⇒ x_D^2 + 144 = 225 ⇒ x_D^2 = 81 ⇒ x_D = 9 (choose the point between A and C).
   So D = (9,12). Then DC = distance from D to C in x-direction = 16 − 9 = 7.

4. Height of trapezium (distance between the parallel sides AB and DC) is 12. The lengths of parallel sides are AB = 25 and DC = 7.
   Area(ABCD) = (1/2)·(AB + DC)·height = (1/2)·(25 + 7)·12 = (1/2)·32·12 = 16·12 = 192.

Final answer
Area of trapezium ABCD = 192 square units.

Question
In triangle PQR, ∆PQR is equilateral. Point S lies on segment QR with QS = (1/3)·QR. Prove that 9·PS^2 = 7·PQ^2.

Diagram cue
The figure shows the altitude from P to QR meeting QR at T. We may use that (derivable from the equilateral triangle) T is the midpoint of QR and PT ⟂ QR.

Method
Drop the perpendicular from P to QR at T. Use right triangles PTQ and PTS:
- express PT (altitude) in terms of PQ,
- find ST from known positions of Q, S, T on QR,
- apply Pythagoras in right triangle PST to get PS^2 in terms of PQ^2,
- multiply to obtain the desired relation.

Working
Let PQ = a. Since ∆PQR is equilateral, all sides equal, so QR = a.

Because PT is the altitude from vertex P to the opposite side QR in an equilateral triangle, T is the midpoint of QR and PT ⟂ QR. Hence
QT = QR/2 = a/2.   (1)

Given QS = (1/3)·QR = a/3. Since Q—T—R with T between Q and R, ST = QT − QS:
ST = a/2 − a/3 = (3a − 2a)/6 = a/6.   (2)

The altitude PT in an equilateral triangle of side a has length
PT = (√3/2)·a.   (3)

Now consider right triangle PST. By Pythagoras,
PS^2 = PT^2 + ST^2
= ( (√3/2·a)^2 ) + ( (a/6)^2 )
= (3/4)a^2 + (1/36)a^2
Bring to common denominator 36:
PS^2 = (27/36)a^2 + (1/36)a^2 = (28/36)a^2 = (7/9)a^2.

Thus PS^2 = (7/9)·PQ^2. Multiply both sides by 9:
9·PS^2 = 7·PQ^2.

Final answer
9·PS^2 = 7·PQ^2, as required.

Question
- Seg PM is a median of triangle PQR. If PQ = 40, PR = 42 and PM = 29, find QR.

Method
- Use Apollonius' theorem for triangle PQR with M the midpoint of QR:
  PQ^2 + PR^2 = 2(PM^2 + MR^2).
- Solve this equation for MR, then double MR to get QR (since M is midpoint of QR).

Working
1. Apply Apollonius' theorem:
   PQ^2 + PR^2 = 2(PM^2 + MR^2).

2. Substitute the given values:
   40^2 + 42^2 = 2(29^2 + MR^2).

3. Compute the squares:
   1600 + 1764 = 2(841 + MR^2).

4. Add the left-hand side:
   3364 = 2(841 + MR^2).

5. Divide both sides by 2:
   1682 = 841 + MR^2.

6. Solve for MR^2:
   MR^2 = 1682 − 841 = 841.

7. Take square root (length is nonnegative):
   MR = √841 = 29.

8. Since M is midpoint of QR, QR = 2 × MR = 2 × 29 = 58.

Final answer
- QR = 58 units.

Question  
Seg AM is a median of ∆ABC. If AB = 22, AC = 34, BC = 24, find AM.

Method  
Use the fact that M is the midpoint of BC and apply Apollonius' theorem for the median:  
AB^2 + AC^2 = 2(AM^2 + BM^2).

Working
1. Since AM is a median, M is the midpoint of BC, so BM = BC/2 = 24/2 = 12.

2. Compute squares:
   - AB^2 = 22^2 = 484
   - AC^2 = 34^2 = 1156
   - BM^2 = 12^2 = 144

3. Apply Apollonius' theorem:
   AB^2 + AC^2 = 2(AM^2 + BM^2)
   484 + 1156 = 2(AM^2 + 144)
   1640 = 2AM^2 + 288

4. Divide by 2:
   820 = AM^2 + 144

5. Solve for AM^2:
   AM^2 = 820 − 144 = 676

6. Take positive square root (length is positive):
   AM = √676 = 26

Final answer  
AM = 26 units.
